% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
LLM-generated text increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, and the resulting recursive chains progressively diverge from human-written text.
We ask whether this drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Studying eight base (pretrained) models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), intermediate, and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$) groups under standard decoding ($t \leq 0.7$), consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, which restricts current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth profiling to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), which suggests that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation across four generators from three families (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that the method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp across generators). Low-temperature improvement is model-dependent (Pythia/OLMo: $+7$--$9$\,pp; Qwen: $0$--$2$\,pp), indicating that depth profiling assumes standard decoding regimes and that the benefit of conservative temperature varies by model family.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
How this evolution proceeds is a fundamental question that connects to both model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad} and data provenance.
Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure the provenance structure of recursive text: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
This is not hypothetical: estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and such text already re-enters training pipelines at scale.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and term this \emph{depth profiling} (characterizing generative provenance from distributional statistics).
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a three-way partition: when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, three \emph{drifting} features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) shift monotonically (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), one \emph{intermediate} feature (entropy std) shows a non-monotonic level shift ($d{=}0.55$), and three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) exhibit negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$).
This is consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable under fixed sampling parameters.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured tri-partition and its exploitation for depth classification have not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds that obscure this intrinsic mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

# ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist

> For EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review. Answers reference specific paper sections.

---

## Section A: Did you describe the limitations of your work?

**A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work?**
Yes. See the dedicated Limitations section (§Limitations, after Conclusion). Key limitations discussed:
- Restricted to base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned models degrade substantially (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1=0.338 vs 0.763 base)
- Generators tested up to 8.2B parameters; frontier models (70B+) untested
- Prompt-type dependent: continuation chains strongest (0.781), paraphrastic weakest (0.671)
- Temperature sensitivity: method reliable at t≤0.7, degrades at t=0.9 (−9.3 to −26.0pp)
- English-only evaluation; non-English generalization untested
- 3-class granularity is the practical ceiling (5-class F1≈0.50)
- Reference model fixed to Pythia-410M (cross-reference spread 0.013 confirms not reference-specific)

**A2. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work?**
Yes. Ethics Statement discusses: (1) no personal/sensitive data involved, (2) method estimates depth not author identity, (3) potential misuse for suppressing legitimate AI-generated content, (4) recommended for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

**A3. Do your abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
Yes. Abstract states: DDR tri-partition finding, 7-feature ensemble binary F1=0.694 under LOGO, and instruction-tuning limitation. Introduction (§1) details the DDR tri-partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis.

---

## Section B: Did you use or create scientific artifacts?

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
Yes. All models cited: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software versions listed in Ethics Statement.

**B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Licenses: Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds).

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifacts is consistent with their intended use?**
Yes. All models used for text generation (intended use). Wikipedia used as seed text (public domain content).

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data/models contain information that names or uniquely identifies people or offensive content?**
Partially. Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated text is model output conditioned on these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?**
Yes. §3 (Method) fully documents: generation chain construction, feature extraction pipeline, evaluation protocol. Appendix provides dataset statistics (Appendix A), per-generator breakdowns, and ablation details. Code/data/models will be released upon publication.

---

## Section C: Did you run computational experiments?

**C1. Did you report the number of parameters in each model used?**
Yes. Table 1 lists parameter counts for all 8 generators (0.6B to 8.2B). Reference model: Pythia-410M (410M parameters). §3.2 specifies exact model identifiers.

**C2. Did you report the computing infrastructure used?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Compute budget: 4× NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total.

**C3. Did you report the average runtime for each approach?**
Partially. Table 2 reports inference time per text (ms/text): 7-feature ensemble 9.7ms, 4-detector ensemble 22.8ms. Training time not separately reported (XGBoost training is negligible, <1min per fold).

**C4. Did you report the evaluation metrics, along with the values and confidence intervals?**
Yes. All primary results include 95% bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Tables 1-2 report CIs. McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons (§4.2). Bonferroni correction applied within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes reported for DDR partition (§4.2).

**C5. Did you report the hyperparameter search strategy?**
Partially. XGBoost uses standard defaults (n_estimators=200, max_depth=6, lr=0.1) without hyperparameter search (§3.4). Appendix C shows alternative classifiers (CORAL, CORN, Frank-Hall) yield comparable performance, confirming discriminative power resides in features not classifier.

**C6. Did you report the number and range of values tried for each hyperparameter?**
N/A. No hyperparameter search conducted; default XGBoost parameters used throughout. Stability confirmed: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds (§3.4).

---

## Section D: Did you use or create data?

**D1. Did you discuss how the data was collected or created?**
Yes. §3.2 describes chain construction: ~1000 Wikipedia seed passages per generator, iterative continuation with fixed prompt template, temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max 256 tokens. 37,058 texts after removing 2,746 chain breaks and 11 short passages. Appendix A provides full dataset statistics.

**D2. Did you report the basic statistics of the data used?**
Yes. §3.2: total texts (37,058), chain breaks (2,746), depth distribution. Appendix A: per-generator breakdown, depth-class counts, token statistics.

**D3. Did you discuss if the data you are using/creating contains personally identifiable information or offensive content?**
Yes. Ethics Statement: "All texts analyzed are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no personal or sensitive data is involved."

**D4. Did you provide the data?**
Will release upon publication. Ethics Statement: "All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication."

---

## Section E: Did you use human annotators or crowdworkers?

**E1-E5.** N/A. No human annotation or crowdsourcing was used. All labels are automatically determined by the generation chain construction process (depth = position in the chain).

Yes. Ethics Statement discusses: (1) no personal/sensitive data involved, (2) method estimates depth not author identity, (3) potential misuse for suppressing legitimate AI-generated content, (4) recommended for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

**A3. Do your abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
Yes. Abstract states: DDR tri-partition finding, 7-feature ensemble binary F1=0.694 under LOGO, and instruction-tuning limitation. Introduction (§1) details the DDR tri-partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis.

---

## Section B: Did you use or create scientific artifacts?

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
Yes. All models cited: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software versions listed in Ethics Statement.

**B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Licenses: Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds).

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifacts is consistent with their intended use?**
Yes. All models used for text generation (intended use). Wikipedia used as seed text (public domain content).

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data/models contain information that names or uniquely identifies people or offensive content?**
Partially. Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated text is model output conditioned on these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?**
Yes. §3 (Method) fully documents: generation chain construction, feature extraction pipeline, evaluation protocol. Appendix provides dataset statistics (Appendix A), per-generator breakdowns, and ablation details. Code/data/models will be released upon publication.

---

## Section C: Did you run computational experiments?

**C1. Did you report the number of parameters in each model used?**
Yes. Table 1 lists parameter counts for all 8 generators (0.6B to 8.2B). Reference model: Pythia-410M (410M parameters). §3.2 specifies exact model identifiers.

**C2. Did you report the computing infrastructure used?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Compute budget: 4× NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total.

**C3. Did you report the average runtime for each approach?**
Partially. Table 2 reports inference time per text (ms/text): 7-feature ensemble 9.7ms, 4-detector ensemble 22.8ms. Training time not separately reported (XGBoost training is negligible, <1min per fold).

**C4. Did you report the evaluation metrics, along with the values and confidence intervals?**
Yes. All primary results include 95% bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Tables 1-2 report CIs. McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons (§4.2). Bonferroni correction applied within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes reported for DDR partition (§4.2).

**C5. Did you report the hyperparameter search strategy?**
Partially. XGBoost uses standard defaults (n_estimators=200, max_depth=6, lr=0.1) without hyperparameter search (§3.4). Appendix C shows alternative classifiers (CORAL, CORN, Frank-Hall) yield comparable performance, confirming discriminative power resides in features not classifier.

**C6. Did you report the number and range of values tried for each hyperparameter?**
N/A. No hyperparameter search conducted; default XGBoost parameters used throughout. Stability confirmed: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds (§3.4).

## Section D: Did you use or create data?

**D1. Did you discuss how the data was collected or created?**
Yes. §3.2 describes chain construction: ~1000 Wikipedia seed passages per generator, iterative continuation with fixed prompt template, temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max 256 tokens. 37,058 texts after removing 2,746 chain breaks and 11 short passages. Appendix A provides full dataset statistics.

**D2. Did you report the basic statistics of the data used?**
Yes. §3.2: total texts (37,058), chain breaks (2,746), depth distribution. Appendix A: per-generator breakdown, depth-class counts, token statistics.

**D3. Did you discuss if the data you are using/creating contains personally identifiable information or offensive content?**
Yes. Ethics Statement: "All texts analyzed are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no personal or sensitive data is involved."

**D4. Did you provide the data?**
Will release upon publication. Ethics Statement: "All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication."

---

## Section E: Did you use human annotators or crowdworkers?

**E1-E5.** N/A. No human annotation or crowdsourcing was used. All labels are automatically determined by the generation chain construction process (depth = position in the chain).

# ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist

> For EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review. Answers reference specific paper sections.

---

## Section A: Did you describe the limitations of your work?

**A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work?**
Yes. See the dedicated Limitations section (§Limitations, after Conclusion). Key limitations discussed:
- Restricted to base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned models degrade substantially (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1=0.338 vs 0.763 base)
- Generators tested up to 8.2B parameters; frontier models (70B+) untested
- Prompt-type dependent: continuation chains strongest (0.781), paraphrastic weakest (0.671)
- Temperature sensitivity: method reliable at t≤0.7, degrades at t=0.9 (−9.3 to −26.0pp)
- English-only evaluation; non-English generalization untested
- 3-class granularity is the practical ceiling (5-class F1≈0.50)
- Reference model fixed to Pythia-410M (cross-reference spread 0.013 confirms not reference-specific)

**A2. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work?**
Yes. Ethics Statement discusses: (1) no personal/sensitive data involved, (2) method estimates depth not author identity, (3) potential misuse for suppressing legitimate AI-generated content, (4) recommended for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

**A3. Do your abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
Yes. Abstract states: DDR tri-partition finding, 7-feature ensemble binary F1=0.694 under LOGO, and instruction-tuning limitation. Introduction (§1) details the DDR tri-partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis.

---

## Section B: Did you use or create scientific artifacts?

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
Yes. All models cited: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software versions listed in Ethics Statement.

**B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Licenses: Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds).

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifacts is consistent with their intended use?**
Yes. All models used for text generation (intended use). Wikipedia used as seed text (public domain content).

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data/models contain information that names or uniquely identifies people or offensive content?**
Partially. Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated text is model output conditioned on these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?**
Yes. §3 (Method) fully documents: generation chain construction, feature extraction pipeline, evaluation protocol. Appendix provides dataset statistics (Appendix A), per-generator breakdowns, and ablation details. Code/data/models will be released upon publication.

---

## Section C: Did you run computational experiments?

**C1. Did you report the number of parameters in each model used?**
Yes. Table 1 lists parameter counts for all 8 generators (0.6B to 8.2B). Reference model: Pythia-410M (410M parameters). §3.2 specifies exact model identifiers.

**C2. Did you report the computing infrastructure used?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Compute budget: 4× NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total.

**C3. Did you report the average runtime for each approach?**
Partially. Table 2 reports inference time per text (ms/text): 7-feature ensemble 9.7ms, 4-detector ensemble 22.8ms. Training time not separately reported (XGBoost training is negligible, <1min per fold).

**C4. Did you report the evaluation metrics, along with the values and confidence intervals?**
Yes. All primary results include 95% bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Tables 1-2 report CIs. McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons (§4.2). Bonferroni correction applied within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes reported for DDR partition (§4.2).

**C5. Did you report the hyperparameter search strategy?**
Partially. XGBoost uses standard defaults (n_estimators=200, max_depth=6, lr=0.1) without hyperparameter search (§3.4). Appendix C shows alternative classifiers (CORAL, CORN, Frank-Hall) yield comparable performance, confirming discriminative power resides in features not classifier.

**C6. Did you report the number and range of values tried for each hyperparameter?**
N/A. No hyperparameter search conducted; default XGBoost parameters used throughout. Stability confirmed: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds (§3.4).

## Section E: Did you use human annotators or crowdworkers?

**E1-E5.** N/A. No human annotation or crowdsourcing was used. All labels are automatically determined by the generation chain construction process (depth = position in the chain).

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth profiling to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), which suggests that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation across four generators from three families (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that the method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp across generators). Low-temperature improvement is model-dependent (Pythia/OLMo: $+7$--$9$\,pp; Qwen: $0$--$2$\,pp), indicating that depth profiling assumes standard decoding regimes and that the benefit of conservative temperature varies by model family.
Tokenizer differences across families may contribute to the observed temperature sensitivity pattern; within-family comparisons (two Qwen models showing consistent robustness) support a family-level effect, but controlling for tokenizer requires further study.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding temperature, we regenerate continuation chains at $t \in \{0.5, 0.9\}$ with fixed nucleus $p{=}0.9$ (matching the default) for four generators spanning three model families: Pythia-2.8B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-0.6B. Evaluation uses the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying temperature (fixed top-$p$\,=\,0.9). Binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. LOGO evaluation; 95\% bootstrap CIs.$^{\ast}$}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc c}
\toprule
Model & Temp & LOGO Binary F1 & 95\% CI & $\rho$(ent.\ mean) \\
\midrule
Pythia-2.8B & 0.5  & \textbf{0.814} & [.798, .828] & $-0.58$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.7  & 0.740 & [.707, .742] & $-0.60$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.9  & 0.480 & [.465, .498] & $-0.30$ \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B & 0.5  & \textbf{0.783} & [.768, .798] & $-0.72$ \\
OLMo-2-1B & 0.7  & 0.695 & [.679, .711] & $-0.60$ \\
OLMo-2-1B & 0.9  & 0.453 & [.437, .469] & $-0.26$ \\
\midrule
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.5  & 0.751 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.7  & 0.751 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.9  & 0.566 & --- & $-0.37$ \\
\midrule
Qwen3-0.6B & 0.5  & 0.711 & [.694, .729] & $-0.67$ \\
Qwen3-0.6B & 0.7  & 0.691 & [.673, .709] & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-0.6B & 0.9  & 0.598 & [.582, .615] & $-0.29$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
\noindent{\footnotesize $^{\ast}$OLMo temperature experiments use OLMo-2-0425-1B (April 2025 release); the original OLMo-2-1B-hf weights used in the main experiments are no longer publicly available.}

Temperature sensitivity is asymmetric and model-dependent. High-temperature degradation ($t{=}0.9$) is universal: all four generators lose $9.3$--$26.0$\,pp in binary F1, with entropy mean's $|\rho|$ weakening to $0.26$--$0.37$ (vs.\ $0.58$--$0.72$ at $t{=}0.5$). Low-temperature improvement ($t{=}0.5$) is model-dependent: Pythia-2.8B and OLMo-2-1B gain $+7.4$ and $+8.8$\,pp respectively, while both Qwen models show negligible change ($0$--$2.0$\,pp). This split tracks model family rather than scale: Qwen3-0.6B (smallest) and Qwen3-1.7B both plateau, while OLMo-2-1B (similar scale to Qwen3-1.7B) benefits substantially. One possible explanation is that Qwen models produce more peaked output distributions at $t{=}0.7$, leaving less room for low-temperature compression to sharpen the depth signal.

The method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ across all tested models. Degradation onset at $t{=}0.9$ defines the practical upper bound, consistent with the hypothesis that elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that DDR exploits (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection*{Per-Generator Performance}

Figure~\ref{fig:per-gen} visualizes per-generator LOGO performance.
Pythia models (1B, 2.8B) achieve highest F1, while larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) show degradation.
The scale effect (larger models $\rightarrow$ lower F1) is consistent with higher-capacity models generating text statistically closer to human writing.

\begin{figure*}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_appendix_per_gen.pdf}
\caption{Per-generator LOGO performance. (a) 8-generator binary and 3-class F1, sorted by binary F1. Dashed lines: pool average. (b) 6-generator LOGO detail heatmap showing the performance spread across model families.}
\label{fig:per-gen}
\end{figure*}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The DDR tri-partition (3 drifting / 1 intermediate / 3 near-stationary) is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Temperature and prompt-type ablations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) support this as a tendency rather than a guarantee: all four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), and the signal varies across prompt types.

Instruction tuning substantially weakens the signal across all three tested families (OLMo, Qwen, Llama).
Within-model 3-class F1 drops 3.7--19.9\,pp (OLMo: 0.575 vs.\ 0.754; Qwen: 0.732 vs.\ 0.769; Llama: 0.544 vs.\ 0.742), while binary F1 changes remain small ($\Delta \leq 3.2$\,pp), indicating that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary.
Under cross-generator evaluation, the degradation is larger (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base).
Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign consistently ($+0.48$ for OLMo and Qwen, $+0.23$ for Llama; all base models ${\approx}{-}0.6$), and 6 of 7 features reverse direction for OLMo and Qwen, 3 of 7 for Llama, consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than destroying the iterative dynamics.
This restricts current applicability to base models; at the document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 suffices for corpus-level flagging but not automated filtering (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).

Three classes represent the practical ceiling (5-class F1 ${\approx}$0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), with the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary as the bottleneck.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift is fully reversible under fixed parameters and leaves distributional shape near-stationary ($d < 0.10$; variance ratios 0.98--1.12).
